transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-20
Start: 09:30 PT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Roth (Redwood SE), Anika Bose (Helios CTO), Tomás Rivera (Helios ML Eng), Linda Cho (Helios Infra)

Summary (auto): Technical deep dive on GPU runtime profiling for on-prem deployment. Topics: kernel selection heuristics, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM behavior, CUDA Graph warmup/instability, KV cache prefetch/eviction strategies, quantization artifacts, and pilot plan for benchmark runs. Agreed next steps and owners.

Topics:
- Profiling tooling (nsys, CUPTI, perf counters)
- Kernel hot spots: attention matmul, rotary sin/cos, softmax, layernorm kernels, gelu approximations
- CUDA Graph stability and warmup effects
- KV cache prefetching heuristics and eviction policies
- Quantization trade-offs int8/4-bit and dequant fusion
- On-prem constraints: NVLink, MIG, PCIe, driver versions

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Samir: hey everybody thanks for joining, uh we wanted to run through a pretty focused profiling session today and leave with a concrete pilot plan. Maya and I will try to keep it technical but also oriented to the infra limits you called out in the pre-call notes.

[00:01:12] Anika: thanks Samir, yeah we, we are really trying to move inference on-prem. Our workload is robotic control and a bunch of multimodal telemetry so latency budget is tight and we can't route payloads to cloud.

[00:02:05] Maya: cool, Tomás can you remind us of the cluster? you mentioned A100s with NVLink, is it 8x per node or 4x?

[00:02:22] Tomás: it's 4xA100 per node, with NVLink pairs between GPUs 0-1 and 2-3; no full mesh. drivers are 525.x, CUDA 11.8. We do have MIG enabled on some nodes but not the ones we'll profile.

[00:03:10] Linda: and we saw some instability when we tried cuda graphs previously — long warmup and occasional OOM spikes when KV cache grows.

[00:03:27] Maya: okay that's helpful — two common themes: cuda graph capture can hide dynamic memory growth, and KV prefetch patterns can cause fragmentation if not sized carefully. We'll walk through the traces and heuristics.

[00:04:10] Samir: quick question — are you using persistent KV across conversations right now, or do you warm per-request?

[00:04:22] Tomás: currently we persist per-session up to 1k tokens and then evict LRU. But we do a full prefix prefetch on session resume which just copies everything to GPU at resume time. that causes stalls.

[00:04:58] Maya: yeah that full prefetch is the low-hanging perf problem. two alternatives: incremental prefetch (opportunistic as tokens are requested) or a hybrid prefetch of recent N tokens + on-demand load of older blocks. incremental keeps GPU memory footprint low and avoids big synchronous copies which interact poorly with cuda graph captures.

[00:05:42] Samir: can you describe what you saw with the cuda graphs? Maya?

[00:05:50] Maya: sure. we saw two failure modes in customers. one, the cuda graph capture is done once and re-used, but if the runtime later needs to allocate extra KV space it fails because the captured graph's scratch allocations are fixed — so you get either a cudaErrorInvalidValue or a silent performance cliff. two, there's warmup: first few iterations after capture show higher latency because kernels JIT/initialize. some engines trigger nvrtc or kernel compilation on first run. that can be mitigated by a deterministic warmup phase.

[00:06:37] Tomás: that matches us — first 20 requests after deploy are slow then steady.

[00:06:45] Maya: for warmup we recommend a short synthetic traffic pattern that exercises long context and varied batch sizes to populate the kernel cache and the cuGraph stable paths. also, capture graphs at several batch-size templates if you have multi-tenancy.

[00:07:20] Anika: what about kernel selection? we heard Redwood runtime picks kernels based on sequence length distribution — how does that interact with TRT-LLM vs vLLM?

[00:07:35] Maya: good question. vLLM often prioritizes memory efficiency and generic kernels which can be great for variable streams, while TensorRT-LLM often uses highly tuned matmul and fused kernels for fixed shapes and quantization-friendly paths. Redwood's runtime uses telemetry to pick between exec paths: a fast fused kernel for short sequences and a memory-optimized kernel for long sequences. the heuristics look at recent sequence histogram, token arrival distribution, and tail-latency SLOs.

[00:08:20] Samir: importantly, TensorRT paths are extremely fast in int8 on supported architectures but can be brittle if attention scaling or rotary doesn't fuse cleanly — we've seen numerical drift on aggressive quant. vLLM CPU-ish paths are more robust but cost more GPU cycles.

[00:09:02] Tomás: can you explain what you mean by "brittle"? we worry about hallucinations or small numeric changes cascading.

[00:09:10] Maya: brittle meaning small rounding errors in int8 matrix multiplications can change beam scoring slightly; for completion tasks that manifests as changed token choice probabilities. usually OK for pragmatic apps but for deterministic control loops you may want int8 only on non-critical heads or use quant-aware calibration with per-channel scales.

[00:09:52] Linda: is there a difference in how KV cache layout is handled between runtime options?

[00:10:00] Maya: yes. TensorRT-LLM often lays out KV as contiguous tensors optimized for GEMM-friendly access — great for bulk matmuls but less flexible for random token reads. vLLM-style runtimes sometimes use sharded KV per layer to allow partial swaps and offload to host. Redwood supports both: we can favor contiguous GPU-resident KV for throughput or sharded/paged KV for memory-limited scenarios.

[00:10:45] Samir: and we added a KV prefetch policy feature: you can set thresholds where the runtime will prefetch the next M tokens when a session crosses a latency threshold, or instead only prefetch the last N tokens. that was the idea we discussed in the pre-call doc.

[00:11:05] Tomás: if we prefetch incrementally, does that increase PCIe chatter? our nodes are PCIe-bound between host and device for certain offloads.

[00:11:18] Maya: it does. the tradeoff is between many small DMA copies vs one large staged copy. We prefer batching small prefetches if they are asynchronous and can overlap compute; otherwise aggregate windows are better. On your NVLink-limited topology, overlapping via NVLink peer copies where possible is key — peer-to-peer is cheaper than host staging.

[00:12:05] Anika: earlier you mentioned memory fragmentation with eviction. what's the mitigation?

[00:12:12] Maya: fragmentation happens when you allocate variable-sized KV blocks during runtime and free them in non-uniform order. two mitigations: reserve big slab allocations per worker and manage offsets internally (reduces fragmentation), or use a compaction pass during low-load periods. slab allocator is simplest for steady-state.

[00:12:40] Samir: another practical note — driver and CUDA mismatches are a big cause of weirdness. Tomás, you're on 525.x; we recommend 535+ for better nvlink peer bandwidth fixes and newer TensorRT integration. we can run compatibility checks in the pilot.

[00:13:05] Tomás: upgrade path is possible but we prefer to test on a slice first.

[00:13:12] Maya: profiling tools to collect: nsys (captures kernels, memcpy, cuda graph activity), CUPTI for low-level counters (L2 hit/miss, sm_efficiency), and host-side perf for CPU stalls. avoid nvprof; it's deprecated. send us the .qdrep and we will annotate.

[00:13:55] Samir: can we talk about quantization artifact detection? how do you validate quality after int8/4-bit?

[00:14:05] Maya: typically we run a small suite: perplexity drift checks, targeted prompt sets that stress rare tokens, and a behavioral test that checks deterministic outputs for critical flows. also, we use per-channel calibration and, where available, outlier-aware quantization for attention heads which are often sensitive. we capture logits differences and map them to user-level metrics — e.g. fraction of responses whose top-3 changed.

[00:14:48] Anika: our concern is control instructions — if quantization alters the command output even occasionally it's problematic.

[00:14:56] Maya: then the plan is conservative: quantize only encoder layers or non-critical heads, do mixed-precision for last N layers, or use float16 for attention output projection. we can test a hybrid 4-bit for FFN with float16 attention as a middle ground.

[00:15:30] Tomás: does Redwood runtime support multiple kernels per layer at runtime? like choose a fused kernel vs a fallback dynamic kernel per request?

[00:15:42] Maya: yes. we have an ExecPath that can switch per-batch based on shape and recent telemetry. switching has overhead so we add hysteresis: only switch after a rollout window or if cost-benefit exceeds a threshold. that helps avoid thrash.

[00:16:20] Samir: let's walk through a hypothetical pilot benchmark: goals are 95th percentile latency under X ms for a 512-token tail, steady throughput of Y tokens/sec, and memory under 90% GPU. we want to test prefetch toggles, graph capture vs no-capture, and int8 vs fp16.

[00:16:45] Anika: what's realistic for our robots? 50ms 95th for 128-token prompts is ideal, 200ms max for 512 tokens.

[00:16:53] Samir: ok we will define concrete SLAs in the spreadsheet. for pilot we recommend: 1) baseline fp16 without cuda graphs, 2) cuda graph capture with warmup, 3) cuda graph + prefetch incremental, 4) int8 with calibration. run each for 30 minutes under synthetic but replayed user traces to simulate token arrival patterns.

[00:17:28] Linda: about telemetry — what traces do you need from our side?

[00:17:34] Maya: nsys .qdrep; GPU utilization and nvlink bw; traces of memcpy and kernel durations; a small set of sample prompts and logs of memory allocations. and if possible, a heapdump of the CUDA allocator at peak.

[00:17:58] Tomás: we can do that. do you need elevated privileges to run nsys on our infra?

[00:18:06] Maya: just sudo to capture system-level counters is enough. we can provide a script.

[00:18:14] Samir: I'd like to highlight a few gotchas we saw in other customers: 1) CUDA Graphs with dynamic attention can cause opaque errors (we add runtime checks to fall back), 2) NVLink partial mesh reduces peer-copy benefits — so topology-aware routing is important, 3) quantization can change latency variability.

[00:18:45] Anika: do you have examples of latency breakdown per token? like tokenization + KV fetch + attention +E2E?

[00:18:52] Maya: yes — we typically see: tokenizer + pre/post processing ~1-3ms, KV fetch (if on-device) sub-ms to a few ms depending on size and peer copy, attention matmul 20-60ms for large layers, FFN 10-40ms, softmax+norm 2-8ms. these vary a lot by model and quantization. we'll annotate your traces with per-kernel timing.

[00:19:40] Tomás: curious about multi-node scenarios — if we split a model across nodes, does Redwood support pipeline parallelism or do you prefer model-sharding?

[00:19:50] Maya: Redwood runtime supports sharded execution and can route requests to shard-aware workers. pipeline parallelism is possible but adds network latency; for on-prem we often prefer tensor/model sharding with NVLink where available. multi-node KV coherence is more complex — we prefer to keep a session's KV local to the worker to avoid cross-node jitter, or use a synchronous pull model with caches.

[00:20:30] Anika: ok what's the timeline for pilot?

[00:20:36] Samir: we propose: gather traces this week, Redwood annotates next week, pilot kickoff the week of Mar 30th.

[00:20:44] Tomás: sounds good. one practical question — what about security for the private pilot? we need SSO and KMS integration.

[00:20:53] Samir: yes, we'll provide a private deployment checklist. SSO via SAML and KMS for key management are standard for Redwood private. we will also provide SOC2 docs.

[00:21:07] Linda: is there a preferred driver/CUDA combo to avoid surprises?

[00:21:12] Maya: we recommend CUDA 12.x + driver 535+ for newest runtime features and better graphs; if you can't upgrade we'll test compatibility.

[00:21:28] Samir: okay let's move to a quick Q&A and then recap action items.

[00:21:33] Anika: will Redwood run the int8 calibration using our data, or synthetic?

[00:21:40] Maya: we can do both. calibration on representative customer data is best but we can start with synthetic edge-case prompts. we will need samples and permission to run calibration offline.

[00:22:02] Tomás: do we risk leaking sensitive prompts in calibration?

[00:22:07] Samir: pilot will be in your private VPC and we can run calibration locally; Redwood doesn't retain raw prompts unless you opt-in. we'll sign an agreement for data handling.

[00:22:22] Maya: final technical note — when testing cuda graphs, also check the behavior under OOM: some runtimes will aggressively pre-alloc and fail early. capture the allocator trace.

[00:22:36] Anika: great, thanks. can you email the runbook and a sample nsys command?

[00:22:42] Samir: yes we'll send that after the call.

[00:22:47] Maya: okay I'll prepare an annotated checklist: profiler commands, expected files, what to look for in the heatmap.

[00:22:58] Samir: recap of next steps and owners — we'll do that in the follow-up email. thanks everyone.

[00:23:05] (Call ends — informal wrap and small talk about robots)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings: "cuda graphs" sometimes transcribed as "cuda caps"; "NVLink" sometimes appears as "N V Link". Speaker labels are consistent but may include small attribution errors in some timestamps.
